particulars: All names, dates, places, ages, sentence lengths, the compensation amount, the court and agency names, the governor, the employer and the book title were dropped.

items.record: The false official record is a criminal conviction for rape and burglary, resting on a victim's eyewitness identification: 'she identified number five — Mr. Cotton — as her attacker.'
items.reading: An administrative finding such as an overpayment or debt, built on bad data from a supplier like an employer report, software output or lab result.
items.loss: This is the basic nature of the false record and of the error behind it: a criminal conviction from a mistaken human memory, not an administrative finding from a faulty data feed.

items.record: The person whose mistake caused the harm was herself the crime victim, sincerely certain and personally harmed: 'Ms. Thompson-Cannino testified and identified him as her attacker.'
items.reading: A neutral outside supplier of data whose input the institution accepted.
items.loss: This is the position of the source of the error: an injured party with her own stake and her own trauma, not a detached third-party provider.

items.record: The misidentification was produced and hardened through police procedure. He appeared in mugshots because of a juvenile record. She first hesitated, 'it is between number four and number five,' then chose after a second viewing with spoken phrases, and repeated the choice at a live lineup.
items.reading: The bad input was 'simply wrong' and accepted as is; there is no account of how the error was formed.
items.loss: This is the step-by-step process by which an uncertain choice became a confident one through repeated identification procedures.

items.record: Weak but similar-looking physical items were used to back up the identification: shoe foam 'that appeared similar,' and a flashlight 'that resembled the one used by the assailant.'
items.loss: This is how circumstantial look-alike evidence was stacked onto the false identification to make it seem confirmed.

items.record: The trial court screened out evidence that pointed the other way. It excluded the other victim's pick of number four 'on grounds that it was not relevant.' Later, the alternate suspect was barred because both women, viewing him out of the jury's presence, 'contended that he was not their attacker.'
items.reading: General institutional 'suppression,' with challenges routed into procedures that presume the record is correct.
items.loss: This is the specific mechanism of suppression: a judge ruling on relevance, and the witnesses' own confidence being used to veto the real culprit.

items.record: The higher court did correct the first trial: the state supreme court 'reversed the convictions and ordered a new trial.' The retrial then made things worse. He was charged with both rapes, the second victim now identified him, 'saying she had been too afraid,' and the sentence was longer. An appeals court then affirmed.
items.reading: The institution does not correct itself; escalation comes from compounding penalties and other files citing the first one.
items.loss: This is the actual sequence of correction followed by renewed and widened error, driven by a witness changing her account, which the reading inverts.

items.record: The physical evidence was preserved for over a decade. At the defense's request, police 'turned over all physical evidence — including the rape kits' for DNA testing.
items.reading: Drifting terrain in which 'the facts become harder to reconstruct as time passes.'
items.loss: This is how time actually worked in the case: preserved evidence plus a new technology made the truth recoverable, not harder to recover.

items.record: Exoneration came from inside the system. The state DNA database matched the real offender, and 'The district attorney and the defense filed a motion to dismiss,' followed by a pardon.
items.reading: Resolution comes from an external shock such as an audit, court, journalist or inquiry, rather than the institution correcting itself.
items.loss: This is the route to resolution: defense-initiated testing and the state's own database, with the prosecution joining to dismiss.

items.record: A real perpetrator existed, was already imprisoned for other assaults, had 'admitted to other inmates that he had committed both crimes,' and later pleaded guilty.
items.loss: This is the presence and role of the actual offender, who was in reach of the system throughout and was later held accountable.

items.record: Afterwards the wrongly convicted man rebuilt his life: he worked at the lab that cleared him, married, had a child, bought land, and received state compensation.
items.loss: This is the aftermath for the wronged person, including compensation and personal recovery.

items.record: The mistaken witness and the man she wrongly accused met, 'became good friends,' toured the country speaking about wrongful convictions and eyewitness reform, and co-wrote a memoir.
items.reading: absent; the parties are described only as entangled in conflict.
items.loss: This is the reconciliation between the source of the error and its target, and their joint turn to public advocacy for reform.
